title: HMRC's £1.04B SME R&D fraud — and the merger it triggered
narrative_md:
**A tax credit designed to reward innovation became a £1 billion-a-year engine for claim-mill fraud before anyone at HMRC noticed.**

HMRC's 2023 mandatory random enquiry programme found that 24.4% of SME R&D tax credit claims in 2020-21 were erroneous or fraudulent — a £1.04 billion hole in the most generous small-business tax relief in the OECD. The Finance Act 2024 merged the SME and RDEC schemes from 1 April 2024 to close the loophole.

R&D tax relief exists in two main flavours in the UK. The Research and Development Expenditure Credit, designed for large companies, pays an above-the-line 20% credit on qualifying spend. The SME scheme, for smaller companies, was historically far more generous — a super-deduction of 230%, with loss-makers able to surrender losses for a 14.5% cash credit.

The asymmetry bred an industry. A cottage trade of 'R&D advisors' — many unregulated, some unqualified — emerged in the late 2010s, approaching SMEs with promises of no-win-no-fee tax rebates. Standard practice: recharacterise routine product development, website work, even bathroom refits as 'qualifying R&D.' The advisors took 20-30% of any payout; HMRC, until 2022, largely processed claims without substantive enquiry.

The Mandatory Random Enquiry Programme, launched in 2022 on 500 SME claims, produced the 24.4% error and fraud rate — far above HMRC's previously-assumed 3.6%. Extrapolated across the scheme, the loss was £1.04 billion in 2020-21 alone. The PAC in a November 2023 hearing called HMRC's previous assurance work 'not credible.' Then-CEO Jim Harra acknowledged the agency had 'underestimated fraud risk.'

The Finance Act 2024 merged the two schemes from 1 April 2024 into a single RDEC-style above-the-line credit at 20%, with a separate enhanced rate for R&D-intensive loss-making SMEs (defined as 30%+ R&D spend ratio, reduced from 40%). The merger removed the cash-credit mechanism that had enabled the claim-mill model and tightened advisor regulation — from 8 August 2023 all claims had to be digitally pre-notified and supported by a named advisor.

HMRC also increased compliance staff by around 300 FTE and began publishing 'refused claim' data. Early signs are encouraging: claim volumes fell 15% in 2024, while average claim values rose — consistent with the fraudulent tail being chopped. Total R&D relief in 2024-25 is projected at £7.5 billion, of which roughly £6.2 billion flows via the new merged scheme and £1.3 billion through the R&D-intensive SME rate.

The episode reveals a pattern in UK tax administration. Generous reliefs are launched with political fanfare — the 2000 R&D scheme, the 2012 Patent Box, the 2014 EIS extensions — but assurance infrastructure lags by years. By the time fraud patterns are measured, the losses are in the billions.

For small genuine innovators — particularly deep-tech startups — the merger has been costly. The blended rate is less generous than the old SME scheme was, and compliance overheads have risen. The PAC's follow-up report in 2024 warned HMRC against 'over-correcting into a system that deters real R&D.'

That tension — between closing fraud and supporting innovation — is now the defining design problem of UK business tax.
